# X11 shim and framework gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so a hack that
  allocates arrays of it (Substrate's two 466 by 466 buffers) is twice the size
  on the host, and host leak numbers are twice the device's. On the device,
  plain `malloc`/`realloc` of about 868 KB reached PSRAM (free PSRAM fell by
  1.74 MB) and came back on restart; internal heap barely moved.
- The board's `malloc` is `CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MALLOC=y` with
  `SPIRAM_MALLOC_ALWAYSINTERNAL=4096`: a block up to 4 KB comes from internal
  RAM and falls back to PSRAM when that is full, and a bigger one goes to PSRAM
  first. An allocation fails only when PSRAM is gone, so a hack's `abort()` on
  a failed allocation is not the risk it looks. The cost of a big pattern is
  internal heap drained to near zero (Celtic read 1,792 B free) and its data
  in slower PSRAM: compare the log's `psram=` with its idle value for the
  overflow.
- `erase_window` (`erase.c`) follows upstream's contract: the first call draws
  nothing and returns a state, so a hack that waits after it (Celtic's 5 s
  `*delay2`) waits on the finished picture. The second call starts a one-second
  wipe (blinds, circle, fizzle or random lines, picked at random), each later
  call draws the next step, and the call after the second is up clears the
  window and returns NULL. Progress comes from `double_time()`, not from the
  call count, so the wipe lasts a second at any step rate. A test or tool
  that does not sleep for a hack's delay must install a clock
  (`xshim_set_clock`), or a wipe never ends. Six hacks never call
  `eraser_free`, so the display tracks live states and the runner releases
  them when a hack stops.
- xlockmore hacks (the 40 that include `xlockmore.h`) need `-DSTANDALONE`,
  which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in
  `hacks/registry.c` with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs
  the hack's `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of
  -2 or above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Galaxy, Drift, Discrete and Flame are built through
  `hacks/<name>_single.c`, which includes the framework headers, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h` (`double` and the libm calls become `float` and
  the `f` versions; the S3's FPU is single-precision only), then the unmodified
  hack; the original `.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1), arcs and pixmap writes live in
  `x11shim/stroke.c`, `arc.c` and `pixmap.c`. Width 0 and 1 keep the old
  `canvas_line` path, so hacks that set no wide width are pixel-identical (every
  hack's frame is pinned in `test_hacks.c`). Braid is the one registered hack
  that draws wide lines (random width 1-7; Maze's width 2 is under
  `HAVE_JWXYZ`). A round-capped segment draws a disc at each end, so
  `stroke.c` keeps each width's rows in a table (widths to 16) rather than
  calling `canvas_fill_ellipse` (which used to do `double` maths per row, in
  software on the S3; see below). A test pins the pixels to
  `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
- `canvas_fill_ellipse` and `canvas_fill_polygon` work in whole numbers, not
  double (the S3 does double in software). The ellipse is exact: a pixel is in
  when `dx2^2 * h^2 <= w^2 * (h^2 - dy2^2)` with distances doubled, and a float
  `sqrt` only starts the search for each row (it is wrong by one at 220 by 21,
  264 by 23, 312 by 25 and 318 by 181, which the tests pin). The polygon steps
  each edge's crossing with a quotient and remainder, no division per row, and
  a pixel on a left edge is in and one on a right edge is out. The old double
  fill was not consistent at exact ties (a 45 degree edge through integer
  vertices): it left stray hatch marks on Qix's thin sliver polygons, so Qix
  (612 pixels) and Pedal (3) re-pinned. Sizes or coordinates past 32768 and
  2^24 keep the double code. On the board (step, before to after): Bouboule
  14.5 to 5.2 ms (27.4 to 36.8 fps), Qix 14.6 to 1.9 ms (37.3 to 70.1 fps),
  Pedal 21.8 to 8.6 ms (it then holds the picture for 5 s).
- Lisa was the counter-example to "the stroker maths is the cost" (#98), and
  then the maths turned out to be the cost after all. Converting a slanted
  segment's ends from int to float moved it by nothing (52.1 ms either way),
  and with the line calls compiled out its step is 5.2 ms, so 47 ms of 52 was
  drawing: 1,396 segments and 6.7k spans a frame at width 2, 13k spans at
  width 8. The guess was a PSRAM cache miss per scattered span. The real
  cost was `fill_convex`: the S3 has no float divide, min, max, floor or
  64-bit conversion, so its per-row loop (two divides, `fminf`, `fmaxf`, two
  `floorf` and two `__fixsfdi` calls a row) was about 3 us a span. It now
  divides each edge's slope once per polygon and uses compares and 32-bit
  `floor_int`. That rounds a few ulps differently from dividing first, which
  moved pixels on a boundary (review of #128): a row whose span ends are within
  rounding of a boundary decision is worked out the old way, and the pixels
  match main's. Test it with each stroke on a cleared canvas
  (`test_wide_strokes_of_random_lines_match_the_pinned_hash`, pinned from main's
  rasteriser): a hash of strokes drawn together missed it, because later strokes
  covered the pixels that differed. Checking every edge of every row cost most
  of the gain (Lisa 43 ms at width 2); checking the two span ends and reusing
  their floors keeps it. On the board Lisa's step went 52.3 to 38.5 ms at width
  2 (14.2 to 17.7 fps) and 85.4 to 60.1 ms at width 8 (9.7 to 12.9 fps), Braid
  125.4 to about 94 ms (8.1 to 9.7 fps) and Deluxe 51.9 to 49.2 ms (19.0 to
  19.9 fps), two rounds each. The width
  sweep on the host (`-DLW=N` with `LINEWIDTH` edited, temporarily) shows the
  cliff is thin to wide: width 1 takes the `canvas_line` path at 0.09 ms, width
  2 is 0.52 ms and width 8 0.85 ms. Look for the same library calls in a
  per-row or per-pixel loop of any hack: `nm` on the object lists them
  (`__divsf3`, `__fixsfdi`, `floorf`, `sqrtf`).
- `canvas_line` (thin lines, width 0 and 1) keeps its endpoints as ints when
  nothing is clipped: it used to convert all four to double and back, which
  the S3 does in software, on every call. Pixels are
  unchanged (`test_lines_inside_the_canvas_match_the_reference` and the
  off-canvas twin draw 20,000 lines each, alone, with `canvas_line` and with a
  copy of the old one in the test file). Compare against a reference copy, not
  a pinned hash, for anything that goes through `clip_line`: its double
  arithmetic rounds differently when the compiler contracts to FMA, and a hash
  taken on one setting fails on the other. On the board XRaySwarm's step went
  21.05 to 13.20 ms (23.2 to 28.3 fps; about 9,700 short lines a step);
  Wormhole 26.9 to 26.0 ms and NerveRot 48.2 to 46.7 ms barely move, since
  they draw far fewer lines and clip some.
  Counting calls on the host (a scratch copy with counters in `canvas_line`,
  `arc_points`, `compute_closed_spline`) put 29 of 109 hacks on `canvas_line`.
  The colour-map builders in `helpers.c` run at start only, so their double
  maths does not matter per frame.
- `canvas_line`'s clip (`clip_line_integer`, `canvas.c`) is the Liang-Barsky
  clip in exact `int64` rationals: it compares the quotients by
  cross-multiplying and rounds each end with one integer divide. The double
  clip (`clip_line`) still decides two cases, and `canvas_line` falls back to
  it for them: an end exactly on a half pixel, where double rounding can land
  either side, and a coordinate past 2^20. The limit comes from an error bound
  (double's error stays near 1e-10, while a rational answer that is not
  exactly on a boundary is at least 1 / 2^22 from it), not from a test: a
  raised limit survives the random tests, since a miss at 10^9 is about one
  in ten million lines. A clipped end sits on the canvas border, so one
  coordinate is an integer and only the other can tie. Pixels match the old
  clip in every reference test, with FMA contraction on and off (a mutant that
  treats every integer as a tie falls back every time and so also passes). On
  the board XSpirograph's step went 11.4 to 7.45 ms (15.2 to 16.8 fps: its
  push, 18.3 to 16.3 ms, now sets the frame) with 404 of 722 lines a step
  clipped; Laser 21.3 to 20.8 ms (52% clipped, but about 270 pixels a line);
  Deco unchanged at 34.3 ms (its own delay holds it at 0.2 fps).
- `arc_points` (`arc.c`) and `compute_closed_spline` (`spline.c`) take a fast
  path and keep the old arithmetic for what the fast path cannot settle. Both
  match the old code point for point in the reference tests, with FMA
  contraction on and off; the pinned frame of every hack is unchanged.
  - `compute_closed_spline` works each point's blend of four controls in
    float (the weights are worked out once, in double, then kept as float) and
    keeps it unless it is within about 1e-3 plus 2e-6 of the largest control
    from a half pixel, where `lround` could go either way; then the original
    double expression decides. Controls past 1e6 in size take the double path
    throughout. The controls are `double` because hacks fill them in, so the
    conversion to float is once a call, not once a point. Goop: step 45.3 to
    35.4 ms (15.9 to 18.9 fps), about 500 points a step.
  - `arc_points` works a run of 16 points from the first by rotating through
    the step between points (four multiplies and two adds, not a divide, `sinf`
    and `cosf`), and a point within 2e-3 plus 4e-5 of the radius from a rounding
    boundary is worked out as before, and the rotation reseeded from it. Angles
    past 32 radians (float's spacing is then near a millionth of a radian) and
    coordinates or radii past 1e6 take the plain loop. The run length is a
    margin: the real drift over a thousand points is about 1e-3 px against a
    tolerance of 0.02 px, so a longer run passes the tests too. Piecewise:
    step 43.4 to 38.6 ms (22.4 to 25.0 fps, about 3,200 arc points a step);
    BoxFit 14.1 to 12.9 ms, with its fps flat (19.1 to 19.2) because its own
    delay sets the frame.
  - A mutant that drops the near-half fallback, one that flips a rotation
    sign, and ones that remove the angle or coordinate limits are each killed
    by the reference tests; a pinned hash would not do here either, since the
    float and double paths can round a half pixel differently.
- `single_precision.h` renames the keyword `double`, not literals: `0.5 * x`
  is still software double. Braid's wrapper includes a copy of the hack with
  every decimal literal suffixed `f`, written at build time by
  `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` (`tools/float_literals.py`). Check a
  wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
  `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` does that for every object in
  the device build, by function: a count in a per-frame function is a literal
  or a macro the header could not reach. It lists none in Galaxy, Discrete,
  Drift, Flame, Substrate or Interaggregate now.
- Four things hide soft double from `single_precision.h`, each found by that
  report. `frand` (`single_frand.h`) and `MAXRAND`, `M_PI`, `M_PI_2` and
  `M_PI_4` (`single_constants.h`) are macros with a decimal literal in their
  body, past the literal pass; both headers are opt-in, since each moves the
  wrapper's frames and pins. Exponent literals (`1e-6`, `1.0E5`) were skipped
  by `float_literals.py` until Drift and Flame showed one each. A struct
  declared with `double` fields before the rename keeps them, so a float
  `corners[j].x * size` plus a `double` `pos.x` is a software add: HexTrail's
  `XYZ` (from `normals.h`) was 94 calls in `draw_hextrail`. Give the hack its
  own float struct under the same name, and `normals.h` another name for the
  double one (`hextrail_single_gl.c`; frames byte-identical). And a trig
  argument that is a big whole number cannot be a float: XSpirograph's second
  angle is millions of degrees and Vines' is an `int` in the billions, so a
  plain `double` to `float` turned both pictures to noise. XSpirograph reduces
  its angles mod 360 in integers at build time (`tools/xspirograph_patch.py`);
  Vines builds `(double) a` as `(long) a`, so its `cos` macro gets the exact
  integer and takes the phase as a 64-bit multiply by 2^64 / 2 pi, wrapping
  into whole turns (`vines_single.c`). Look at a frame before trusting a
  float build of anything whose angles grow. To find the line of a stray
  promotion, add `-Wdouble-promotion -fsyntax-only` to a file's compile
  command in `firmware/compile_commands.json` (`pio run -e stopwatch -t
  compiledb`; delete the file afterwards, it upsets the editor).
- A colour pixmap is a `Canvas`, and every drawing primitive draws on the
  drawable it is given (`xshim_target` in `pixmap.c`); `None` draws nothing,
  and a bitmap takes only `XCopyArea`, `XCopyPlane` and filled rectangles and
  polygons (see below). One exception still draws on the window whatever
  it is given: Deluxe's wrapper, which calls `stroke_circle(dpy->canvas,
  ...)`. No
  registered hack drew into a pixmap before this (the `HAVE_JWXYZ` wrappers
  and Deluxe's `doubleBuffer: False` turn double-buffering off), so keep
  those: a back buffer costs 434 KB and a full-frame copy, and dirties every
  row. Without a
  clip mask, `XCopyArea` copies colour rows whole with `canvas_paste_rect`. A
  pixmap wider or taller than `INT16_MAX` is `None` (the canvas's dirty spans
  are `int16_t`). Truchet draws into one (issue #61). The display tracks every
  pixmap a hack holds and the runner frees what a stopped hack left behind
  (Pacman leaked 514 KB per start). The GC keeps its own copy of a clip mask
  because hacks free the pixmap right after `XSetClipMask`. There is no PNG
  decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads
  the raw blob described in `ximage-loader.h`, made by
  `tools/make_logo_blob.py` (`uv run`, needs Pillow). Pacman's sprites,
  XMatrix's large glyph sheets and the grab image are built with `--deflate`
  ("565Z", issue #102): 1.39 MB of flash saved, unpacked into a temporary
  buffer while the image loads (Pacman's is 522 KB of PSRAM, briefly), by the
  ROM's `tinfl` on the device and zlib on the host, so host builds link `-lz`
  (`platformio.ini`, `probe_hacks.py`, `gl_budget.py`). Host tests cover only
  zlib. XMatrix's small sheets are never drawn at 466 px: their generated
  headers `#define` them to the large ones. The `logo_180`/`360`
  headers are aliases of the 50 px data, as a 466 px screen only picks 50.
  `XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repo root) swaps the logo for a local
  image, shrunk to fit 50 px, without committing it: `firmware/logo_override.py`
  writes the header into the build dir, where `maze_patched.c` finds it
  before the committed one. Unset, it deletes that header. Needs `uv`. A
  third-party logo kept under `vendor/` stays out of git that way. The WorkOS
  icon is `vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png`. A plain flash with it is
  `unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` then `XS_LOGO=vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png
  pio run -e stopwatch -t upload`: build flags stick, so a leftover pin from
  an earlier probe would survive. The logo shows in Maze only.
- A wide circle through `XDrawArc` is a polyline of about a thousand wide
  segments, each filled a row at a time: 40 times the fills of a ring, and the
  polyline leaves gaps in it. `stroke_circle` (`x11shim/stroke.c`) fills the
  ring in two spans a row. Only Deluxe's wrapper calls it, and it does full
  circles only: Pacman's wall arcs are quarters and Celtic's wide strokes are
  lines, so they still take the stroker. The polyline's gaps were float
  rounding, not the joins or the point spacing: a pixel centre exactly on an
  edge shared by a segment quad and the join wedge at its end (any 45 degree
  edge through integer vertices) fell out of both, because float32 put the
  quad's right edge at 57.499996 for 57.5. `fill_convex` now takes a right
  edge inclusive to within `EDGE_SLACK` (1e-3; 1e-7 fails the test, 1e-5
  passes), and `test_wide_full_arc_fills_every_pixel_in_its_band` pins it. It
  moved five pinned frames by 0 to 33 pixels each (Deluxe, Forest, Rotor,
  Compass, Celtic). Pacman is not affected: its `wallwidth` is 1 at this
  size, which takes the thin-line path. Celtic's overpaint (about 50 paints a
  pixel a step on the host, 46% of its line draws zero-length) is still open
  in #56. Changing shared stroke code can move pinned frames: look at them and
  ask Rod. The pin test hashes steps 50, 100, 150 and 200 with a fake clock
  that carries across hacks, so a dump program does not reproduce its frames:
  write them from the test itself.
- `XshimGC.alpha` (0 is opaque, 1 to 31 is the weight out of 32) makes the
  wide-line code in `stroke.c` blend over the canvas instead of overwriting it;
  fills, `canvas_line` and the other primitives ignore it. The canvas is
  byte-swapped RGB565, so the blend swaps each pixel and back. A shape of
  overlapping pieces (a polyline, a round cap and its segment) sets bits in a
  mask the size of the canvas (a 27 KB `calloc` per shape, freed at the end)
  and blends it once, or the overlaps blend twice and a star's corners show
  as bright diamonds. A failed `calloc` falls back to blending piece by piece.
  Setting `alpha` takes a wrapper, as in `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`.
- Don't declare `xrealloc` or `xmalloc` in the shim: cloudlife defines its own
  static `xrealloc`, which would clash.
- `XGetImage` and `XPutImage` (`ximage.c`) move 32-bit ZPixmap images (the raw
  RGB565 value in each) to and from the window or a colour pixmap; a bitmap
  format, `None` or an empty region gives NULL. XMatrix flips its glyph sheets
  through them. Overrunning a row's right edge wraps onto the next row without
  AddressSanitizer seeing it, so a clip test must look at that next row.
- `XPutImage` copies a 16-bit image a row at a time with `memcpy`; other
  depths keep the per-pixel loop, since they keep only the low 16 bits (#82).
  ad-flyingtoasters at 2x: step 29.3 to 6.7 ms, 22.3 to 28.5 fps; at 1x: step
  15.9 to 3.7 ms. Fireworkx draws its own squares and did not change.
- `image_data_to_pixmap` accepts a NULL width, height or mask pointer (XMatrix
  passes no mask, and a NULL mask used to crash it on start); with no mask
  pointer no mask is made.
- `XClearWindow` clears to the colour `XSetWindowBackground` last set
  (default 0), and `xshim_release_pixmaps` resets it when a hack stops: the
  display outlives the hack, and Hexadrop's colour once turned Pyro's clear
  into a solid fill. No key events ever arrive, so `XLookupString` finds no
  characters, and an Xt timer (`X11/Intrinsic.h`) is never made.
- The shim still draws nothing into a depth-1 pixmap and draws every GC as
  `GXcopy`; it only remembers the function in `gc->function` now (GXcopy, GXor,
  GXxor). Halo and Moire2 handle both inside their own wrappers
  (`halo_planes.h`, `moire2_planes.h`).
- `screenhack.h`'s `frand` has a `1.0` inside its macro body, so the float
  literal pass cannot reach it and a single-precision wrapper still divides in
  double (software on the S3; `nm` shows `__divdf3`). `hacks/single_frand.h`
  redefines it in float; it is opt-in, because the older wrappers' frame hashes
  are pinned with the original.
- Added for the second batch, each test-first: 16-bit ZPixmap `XImage`s
  (canvas-order pixels, like every other value the shim hands out: `XAllocColor`
  -> `XPutPixel` -> `XPutImage` keeps the pixel; `XPutImage` does not swap.
  Only `lowrez_put_image` swaps, because Fireworkx writes ordinary RGB565
  bytes straight into the image data) and
  `ImageByteOrder`; `CoordModePrevious` in `XFillPolygon`, `XDrawLines` and
  `XDrawPoints`; `XCreatePixmapFromBitmapData` (X bitmap data is least
  significant bit first); a spline of our own (`spline.c`, not xscreensaver's);
  `XQueryColor`; `DisplayOfScreen` (the display opened last); the fill-rule,
  fill-style and stipple constants (accepted, ignored: fills are solid and
  even-odd); and `XSetFunction` and `jwxyz_XSetAlphaAllowed` (no-ops).
- Added for the third batch, each test-first: `ya_random` (the C library's
  `random()`, so `ya_rand_init` seeds it); `make_color_ramp` (the short way
  round the hue wheel, there and back when `closed_p`; ours, not
  xscreensaver's); `visual_depth` (always 16); `xshm.h` with
  `create_xshm_image`, `put_xshm_image` and `destroy_xshm_image`, which are a
  zeroed 16-bit `XImage` and `XPutImage` (`x11shim/xshm.c`); the arrow and page
  keysym constants (X's values; no key event ever arrives); and `glOrtho` (see
  `gl.md`). The Edit tool drops a trailing space from `old_string` and
  `new_string`: an edit that ends at a space in `platformio.ini`'s
  `build_src_filter` glued two entries together (it still built, which hid it).
- `allocate_alpha_colors` still finds no colour planes, so a hack that wants
  transparency (Qix, Goop) falls back to opaque layers and prints "couldn't
  allocate any color planes" on the host.
- The comment in `xshim.h` saying `XPutImage` byte-swaps a 16-bit image has
  been stale since commit 272ad6a: an `XImage` holds canvas-order pixels. A
  hack that builds its own 16-bit image must `px_swap` its pixels first.
- Added for the 2026-10-12 batch, each test-first: `XCopyArea` from the
  window (onto itself, rows moved with `memmove` in the order that reads each
  first, or into a pixmap); `XSetGraphicsExposures`; `make_color_loop` (ours);
  `grabclient.h` with `load_image_async_simple`, which finishes at once, with
  the grab image painted if one is set (below); `thread_util.h`, a pool that
  runs each thread in turn on the caller, as upstream does without pthreads;
  `visual_pixmap_depth`; `XCharStruct`; and `image_data_to_ximage` (RGBA
  bytes, bottom row first). `screenhack.h` now includes `visual.h` and
  `grabclient.h`, as upstream's does.
- `tools/wire_hack.py` puts a new hack before the After Dark toasters'
  `#ifdef` in the registry, the expected list and `kBaseline`.
- Added for the 2026-10-12 second batch, each test-first: `XClearArea` (the
  window background, clipped; a width or height of 0 runs to the window's
  edge; Worm), `XMaxRequestSize` (65535, so Lisa batches about 32,000 points a
  call) and the `LineOnOffDash` and `LineDoubleDash` constants (accepted;
  lines still draw solid; Penrose uses them only in its monochrome path). The
  scorer's gap list was wrong for Triangle (`free_colors` and
  `make_smooth_colormap` exist; its xlockmore include chain just does not
  reach `colors.h`, so `hacks/triangle_colors.c` includes `screenhack.h`
  first) and XRaySwarm (`initTime` is the hack's own, behind
  `HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY`, which upstream takes from `config.h`:
  `hacks/xrayswarm_time.c` defines it). Putting `colors.h` in the shim's
  `screenhackI.h` would have fixed Triangle for all but changes what every
  xlockmore hack sees, so it is Rod's call.
- `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` fill a depth-1 pixmap now (Rocks): a bit
  is set where the GC's foreground is odd and cleared where it is even, and the
  clip mask and the GC's function are ignored. The polygon is even-odd, a pixel
  being in when its centre is, in float. Other primitives still draw nothing on
  a bitmap. Halo, Moire2 and Goop keep their own planes or layers and did not
  move.
- `xshim_set_grab_image` (`grabclient.h`) gives `load_image_async_simple` a
  picture to paint over its target the next time a load starts: scaled to cover
  and cropped evenly at the sides (a 4:3 screenshot on the square screen loses
  its left and right edges), mask ignored, finishing at once as before. `main.cpp`
  sets it from the header `firmware/grab_image.py` writes into the build
  directory: `firmware/assets/grab-image.png` (Rod's choice: the Windows 95
  screenshot from guidebookgallery.org, committed at his say-so, with a
  notices section), or `XS_GRAB_IMAGE=<file>`, and `XS_GRAB_IMAGE=none` builds
  without. It is stored at up to 466 pixels (a 466 by 350 blob was 340
  KB of flash, 48 KB since it was deflated in #102: the build had gone from
  2.39 MB to 2.74 MB, 87.0% of the app partition). The host tests set their
  own picture, so a pin never depends on the local file; `dump` sets it when
  the header exists. DecayScreen is unpinned for that reason
  (`test_decayscreen_melts_the_grab_image`). Boxfit's `grab` mode, off by
  default, would get the picture too.
- `make_smooth_colormap` follows upstream's behaviour (written from scratch, not
  copied): two to five random points in hue, saturation and value, repicked if
  adjacent ones are close or the average is too grey or dark, joined in a closed
  path with colours spaced by edge length. The first version always spanned the
  hue wheel at high saturation and value, so Triangle and 23 other pinned hacks
  were a bright rainbow.
- The Xft stand-in (`xft.h`, `xft.c`, `xft_font.h`; ours) draws 8-bit coverage
  glyphs, blended over the canvas pixel by pixel (the canvas is byte-swapped
  565, so each pixel is swapped, weighed in 8-bit channels and packed again),
  clipped in 64 bits and marked dirty once a glyph. It ignores the GC's clip
  mask, as Xft does. The glyph data is baked from `assets/fonts/` at 12, 16,
  20 and 24 pixels (`font_atlas.py`): the tables cost about 57 KB of flash
  (87.0% of the app partition became 88.8% with XJack), and a size is picked
  by the number at the end of a font name. `screenhack.h` does not include
  `xft.h`: a hack gets it through a wrapper (`hacks/xjack_xft.c`). With no
  font installed a hack gets a blank one (advance, no ink), because XJack
  `abort()`s on none and `test_pyro` and `test_push_present` run every hack.
- The runner never sends a hack a reshape, and `XClearWindow` clears to
  black unless the hack calls `XSetWindowBackground`, where xscreensaver's
  `screenhack.c` sets the window background from the `background` resource and
  sends a reshape after init. A hack that depends on either needs a wrapper
  (XJack's `xjack_init_on_paper`); doing it in the runner would change what
  every hack sees, so it is Rod's call. Any other registered hack with a
  light `background` that calls `XClearWindow` may have the same fault.
- The shim's `screenhack.h` does not include `screenhackI.h` (upstream's
  does), so plain hacks and xlockmore hacks see different headers. Put a
  macro upstream defines in `screenhackI.h` for every hack into a small
  header both include, as `nls.h` (`_()` and `gettext`) is.

content.text:
The near-static variant builds, and the build log shows no errors. It isn't flashed yet.

- **What it does:** `-DUP_STATIC` adds `*speed: 0.01` to Unknown Pleasures' overrides in `registry.c`. The hack then adds a new row only about every 120 s. The picture is nearly identical from frame to frame, but it still redraws and pushes at the usual 5 Hz, because pushes follow dirty marks and the hack redraws its whole scene.
- **One variable:** this build doesn't include `CABC_OFF`, so the panel is in its default state, as in the original clips.
- **Binary check:** the `*speed: 0.01` string is in the ELF.
- **Commit:** `0284ecc` on `fix/68-cabc-off-probe`.

**How to read the result** (baseline: dimmest band 0.86 on the default build)
- **Dip survives:** it's the act of writing to the panel, so it's the bus, supply or panel, not the picture.
- **Dip gone:** it depends on the pixels changing, which points back at the scene.

One thing to look for when you film: the lines will barely move. If you see a scrolling plot, the override didn't take, so tell me.

content.text:
In the near-static build the dip is gone: the whole display never falls below 0.990 of its median across 2,440 frames, and the detector finds no dip events. What I can't yet show is that the board was pushing during the clip.

| Measure | IMG_5864 (CABC off, moving) | IMG_5865 (static, `*speed: 0.01`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Whole-display minimum | about 0.88–0.91 per push | **0.990** |
| Dip events found | 23, every 24 frames (5 Hz) | **0** |
| Frames below 0.97 | 2–3 per update | **0** |
| Random-window noise floor | 0.991 | 0.993 (worst 0.986) |

- **Camera:** it drifted at most 1 px, so the clip is steady.
- **What the code says:** the push follows dirty marks, and the GL layer marks the box around everything TinyGL draws. It doesn't compare pixels, so a redrawn identical frame should still push at 5 Hz. That's from reading the code, not a measurement.
- **Why it matters:** if the board wasn't pushing, "no dip" would only mean nothing was written. The video can't tell, because the picture doesn't change.

I'd like to open the serial port for a few seconds to read the run log's `fps=`, `push=` and rows pushed, which would confirm 5 Hz pushes of a full frame. May I? I'd use `tools/serial_capture` on `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401`.

If the log confirms pushes, the finding is: writing identical pixels at 5 Hz doesn't dim the panel, and the dip depends on the pixels changing. That would drop the supply and bus theories and point at something content-driven. Mean brightness would fall back as the lit-pixel count changes, so the next probe would split "lines move" from "more or fewer lit pixels". I'd propose that after the serial check.

serial_capture.py
"""Reads the StopWatch's serial log into a file for a number of seconds.

    .venv/bin/python -I tools/serial_capture.py <out-file> <seconds> [port]

Opening the port resets the board (a random hack starts, the overlay returns to
nothing), and a flash or a crash makes the port go away and come back, so this
reopens it in a loop. DTR and RTS are set low before each open: a reopen loop
without that once parked the chip in its bootloader. Run it in the background with absolute paths; background
shells ignore `cd`. The `run <hack> fps= step= push= ...` lines are explained in
AGENTS.md ("Serial log").
"""

import sys
import time

import serial

DEFAULT_PORT = "/dev/cu.usbmodem112401"


def capture(out: str, seconds: float, port: str = DEFAULT_PORT) -> None:
    end = time.time() + seconds
    with open(out, "wb") as f:
        while time.time() < end:
            s = serial.Serial()
            s.port = port
            s.baudrate = 115200
            s.timeout = 1
            s.dtr = False
            s.rts = False

content.text:
Pushes happened during the clip, so the "no dip" result stands. The run log from the static build shows a full-frame push every cycle:

```
run UnknownPleasures fps=5.0 step=167.9ms push=32.3ms sync=1.7ms rows=466
run UnknownPleasures fps=4.8 step=169.2ms push=32.3ms sync=10.3ms rows=466
```

- **Rows:** `rows=466` is a full frame, and the push is 32.3 ms, identical to the moving build's push.
- **Rate:** 4.8–5.0 fps is the same 5 Hz as the clip with the dips.
- **Sync:** `sync=` is the TE wait, so the synced push was running.
- **Board state:** opening the port reset the board, as the tool warns. It rebooted on the same static build and is still on it.

So with identical pixels the board writes a full frame to the panel at 5 Hz, and the screen doesn't dip. The dip isn't caused by writing as such, so the supply sagging with bus and PSRAM load, and the panel reacting to a long QSPI transfer, are now unlikely. The same push duration and bus traffic produce no dip when the pixels are unchanged. CABC off also didn't remove it (with the caveat that I couldn't confirm the register was accepted).

That leaves something that depends on the pixels changing. Rod's by-eye report fits: the sparse build (fewer lit pixels) doesn't dim.

**Next experiment:** film the sparse build, 20 rows of 50 points, at its usual 7.4–7.6 fps, and measure its dip with the same method. This turns your by-eye observation into a number.
- If the dip shrinks with fewer lit pixels, the cause is something like a power limit in the panel that depends on how much light is on screen.
- If it's still 0.86 with fewer pixels, the cause is the scene changing, not how much of it is lit.

A small registry override covers this build, behind a flag like the others. Shall I build it?

# /// script
# dependencies = ["numpy"]
# ///
import sys, numpy as np
S = sys.argv[1]
a = np.fromfile(S + "/s540.raw", np.uint8).reshape(-1, 960, 540)
print("frames", len(a))
def shift(ref, cur):
    w = np.outer(np.hanning(ref.shape[0]), np.hanning(ref.shape[1]))
    F = np.fft.fft2(ref * w) * np.conj(np.fft.fft2(cur * w))
    r = np.fft.ifft2(F / (np.abs(F) + 1e-6)).real
    y, x = np.unravel_index(r.argmax(), r.shape)
    h, wd = r.shape
    return (y if y < h // 2 else y - h, x if x < wd // 2 else x - wd)
for n, (y0, y1, x0, x1) in {"TR": (0, 50, 400, 540), "TL": (0, 50, 200, 320), "L": (180, 330, 0, 50)}.items():
    ref = a[0, y0:y1, x0:x1].astype(np.float32)
    sh = np.array([shift(ref, a[i, y0:y1, x0:x1].astype(np.float32)) for i in range(0, len(a), 20)])
    print(n, "dy", sh[:, 0].min(), sh[:, 0].max(), "dx", sh[:, 1].min(), sh[:, 1].max())
cx, cy, h, nb = 300, 300, 150, 12
roi = a[:, cy - h:cy + h, cx - h:cx + h].astype(np.float32)
bands = roi.reshape(len(a), nb, 2 * h // nb, 2 * h).mean(axis=(2, 3))
whole = roi.mean(axis=(1, 2)); whole /= np.median(whole)
x = whole - whole.mean(); ac = np.correlate(x, x, "full")[len(x) - 1:]; ac /= ac[0]
print("autocorr peaks:", [(k, round(float(ac[k]), 2)) for k in sorted(range(8, 60), key=lambda k: -ac[k])[:5]])
print("whole-display: min %.3f ; frames below 0.97: %d" % (whole.min(), (whole < 0.97).sum()))
ev = []
for i in range(8, len(whole) - 8):
    if whole[i] < 0.985 and whole[i] == whole[i - 5:i + 6].min() and (not ev or i - ev[-1] >= 8): ev.append(i)
print("dip events:", len(ev), ev[:14]); print("gaps:", list(np.diff(ev))[:20])
per = int(np.median(np.diff(ev))) if len(ev) > 2 else 16
out = []; dep = []
for i in ev:
    if i + per - 2 < len(a):
        s = bands[i + per // 2 + 1:i + per - 2].mean(axis=0)   # settled: after the dip, before the next push
        out.append((bands[i - 2:i + 5] / s).min()); dep.append(whole[i])
print("period", per, "| dimmest band vs settled: mean %.3f  min %.3f  max %.3f over %d" % (np.mean(out), min(out), max(out), len(out)))
rng = np.random.default_rng(1); nf = []
for _ in range(300):
    c = int(rng.integers(20, len(a) - 30)); 
    if min(abs(c - e) for e in ev) < 6: continue
    s = bands[c + 7:c + 10].mean(axis=0); nf.append((bands[c - 2:c + 5] / s).min())
print("no-push windows: median %.3f  5th pct %.3f  min %.3f" % (np.median(nf), np.percentile(nf, 5), min(nf)))
print("frames below 0.97 per update:", [int((whole[i - 4:i + 6] < 0.97).sum()) for i in ev][:20])
EOF

content.text:
The sparse build dips less: the dimmest band averages **0.943** against 0.862 on the dense build. That's consistent with Rod's by-eye report.

| Build | Dimmest band vs settled | Whole-display minimum | Push rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Default, CABC off (IMG_5864) | 0.862 (23 updates) | about 0.88–0.91 | 5 Hz |
| Near-static (IMG_5865) | no dip | 0.990 | 5 Hz |
| Sparse, 20×50 (IMG_5866) | **0.943** (40 updates, range 0.93–0.96) | 0.948 | 7.5 Hz (gaps of 16 frames) |

- **Camera:** drift was 1 px or less.
- **Dip depth:** the sparse dip is about 5.7% against 13.8% on the dense build, roughly 0.4 of it.
- **Noise floor:** this clip is noisier. Windows with no push give a median of 0.992, with a 5th percentile of 0.967 and a minimum of 0.954. Thin, widely spaced lines move between my bands more. All 40 dips sit below that floor's 5th percentile, so the dip is real, but the 0.4 ratio is approximate.
- **Perception:** a 6% dip at 7.5 Hz is below what Rod sees. 14% at 5 Hz is above it.

**What the three clips say together**
- **Not the write itself:** the static build pushes the same 466 rows in 32 ms, so the dip isn't the write, bus load, supply or CPU load.
- **Not lit pixels:** the static build lights as many pixels as the dense one and doesn't dip.
- **Changed pixels:** the sparse build has about half as many lines and changes about half as many pixels, and its dip is about 0.4 of the dense one. A dip that scales with how many pixels change fits all three clips. This is an inference from three clips, not a measurement of changed pixels.

I don't know the physical mechanism. I'd rather not guess at it.

**Options for the next step**
1. **Alternating-frames probe (my recommendation).** Pushing the same picture, then the same picture shifted 1 px, and so on, keeps the load identical and varies only how much changes. It separates "pixels changed" from "pixels changed a lot". Needs a build and a flash.
2. **Take the practical route.** Stay on the dense default and look at what reduces the change per update (smaller steps, softer lines, or a middle density such as 30 rows). If the dip follows changed pixels, that's the lever, and I'd measure each variant on film.
3. **Stop here.** Close #68 with what we've learned: the dip follows content and it's panel-side. I'd update `device-display.md` and put the three clips' numbers on the issue, with your approval for posting.

I'd do option 1 first, since a clean answer tells us whether option 2 can work at all. Which would you like? The board is still on the sparse build, so tell me before you want it back on plain main.

content.text:
The alternating-frames probe builds with no errors. It isn't flashed. The commit is `96fbecd` on `fix/68-cabc-off-probe`.

**How it works**
- With `-DALT_PROBE`, `present()` copies the canvas into a spare 434 KB PSRAM buffer before the TE wait, and the push reads that copy.
- Even frames are copied as they are. Odd frames are shifted right by `ALT_SHIFT_PX` pixels (default 1), with black filling the vacated column.
- The copy runs on every frame, so CPU and PSRAM load are the same whatever the shift.
- Built with `-DUP_STATIC`, the hack's own motion is removed. What changes between pushes is only how many pixels differ.
- It builds without errors. I haven't run it. On the panel you should see the plot jitter by 1 px at about 4–5 Hz.

**Reading the result**

| Shift | What it tests | Expected if the dip follows changed pixels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 px (this build) | Every lit pixel moves | A dip returns, probably close to the dense build's 0.86 |
| 0 (control) | The copy itself | No dip, like IMG_5865 |

I'd flash the 1 px build first and film it. If a dip returns, run the 0 px control afterwards to rule out the copy as the cause. If no dip appears at 1 px, the theory is wrong or one pixel is too small a change. A larger shift would then be the next try.

The step is longer now, because the copy adds about 25 ms, so the push rate will be nearer 4.3 Hz. The TE wait is placed after the copy, so the push still starts at the same point in the panel's refresh.

Can I flash the 1 px build to `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401`? It replaces the sparse build currently on the board.

content.text:
The shift is real in the video, and the dip isn't there. That means my changed-pixels theory is wrong.

**Control:** the display's horizontal position alternates between about −0.1 px and +0.6 px at video scale, holding each state for about 28 frames. That's one flip per push, so the 1 px shift reached the panel, and about 1.05 video px is one native pixel.

| Build | Pixels changed per push | Dimmest band vs settled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default, CABC off (IMG_5864) | lines move a few px, scene evolves | **0.862** |
| Sparse, 20×50 (IMG_5866) | about half as many | **0.943** |
| Near-static (IMG_5865) | almost none | no dip (0.990) |
| **Alternating 1 px shift (IMG_5867)** | **every lit pixel, every push** | **0.977, inside the noise** (no-push windows: median 0.994, 5th percentile 0.980) |

In the alternating build every lit pixel moves on every push. That's more change than the default build has. Yet the whole-display minimum is 0.962, and only 5 frames fall below 0.97, against 2–3 frames at every push in the dense moving clip.

So what the dip needs is neither the write, nor the amount of pixel change, nor how much is lit. The two builds with no dip both freeze the scene (`*speed: 0.01`). The two with a dip both let it evolve, and the sparse one evolves less and dips less. Differences I haven't ruled out are that the copy changes the push path, or a camera artefact.

**A hypothesis that fits all four clips:** the panel limits brightness by the frame's average picture level (APL), as many AMOLED drivers do to cap power, separate from the CABC register I turned off. If the moving picture's total lit amount changes from frame to frame, the panel would re-level after each push and dim for a moment. A 1 px shift keeps the total the same, and the static scene doesn't change it. I haven't tested this.

**Two cheap ways to test it**
1. **Host check, no flash.** Measure the total lit amount of successive frames of the default dense build. If it varies by only about 1%, APL can't explain a 14% dip and I drop it. If it varies by several per cent, it's plausible.
2. **Device probe.** Take the static build and alternate full brightness with about 90% brightness on odd frames. This changes only the lit total, so a dip returning would point at APL. It needs a build and a flash.

I'd do 1 now, since it costs a few minutes and no flash, then 2 only if it survives. Shall I go ahead with the host check? The board is still on the alternating-frames build.

content.text:
The host test rules out APL as the cause. `dump_main.c` is back to the committed version and the tree is clean.

| Build (host, one frame every 0.2 s or 0.133 s) | Mean total brightness | Frame-to-frame change (mean / max) | Device dip |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dense default | 3.63 M | **0.18%** / 0.82% | **0.862** (14%) |
| Sparse 20×50 | 1.84 M | **0.54%** / 3.75% | 0.943 (5.7%) |

- **Dense:** the total light in successive pushed frames differs by only 0.18% on average, and 0.8% at worst. A 14% dip can't come from a 0.2% change in picture level.
- **Sparse:** it varies about three times more between frames, yet dips less. That's the opposite order from what an APL effect would give.
- **Lit pixels:** about 23.8 k dense against 12.2 k sparse, so the sparse build has half the light, in line with the dips' size ratio.
- **Caveats:** this is the host's rendering, not a camera-measured frame. The simulated clock advances 0.2 s per frame, but the hack's real timing on the board may differ slightly.

**Where that leaves us**
- Not the write, bus load or CPU load: the static build does all of that.
- Not how many pixels change: the alternating 1 px build changes more than the moving one.
- Not how much is lit: the static build is as bright and doesn't dip.
- Not CABC, with the caveat that I couldn't confirm the panel accepted `0x55`.
- Not the picture's average level: frames are almost constant.

The dip appears only when the scene evolves smoothly (sub-pixel movement), and it's bigger when more lines move. I don't have a mechanism for that. The clips so far don't separate real light from what the camera does with moving content, though Rod does see the pulsing by eye.

**What I'd try next:** the dense moving build with the copy path in and a shift of 0 (`-DALT_PROBE -DALT_SHIFT_PX=0`, no `UP_STATIC`). The alternating build changed two things at once: it froze the scene and it added a copy before the TE wait. This build restores the moving scene and keeps the copy.
- If the dip vanishes, it depends on the push path, meaning what ran just before the push or where the data sat in memory. That points back at the supply or the cache.
- If the dip stays, it's the evolving content, and the next step is the sub-pixel intensity changes in the lines.

It's built from code that already exists, so it's a quick build and one flash. Shall I build it, or would you like to take a different direction?

content.text:
The dip is still there with the copy path in and no shift, so the push path isn't the cause.

| Build | Pushes | Dimmest band vs settled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dense default, CABC off (IMG_5864) | 24 frames apart | 0.862 |
| **Dense + copy path, shift 0 (IMG_5868)** | **28 frames apart** | **0.847** (20 steady updates, range 0.836–0.858) |
| Near-static (IMG_5865) | 24 | no dip (0.990) |
| Alternating 1 px, static (IMG_5867) | 28 | no dip (0.977, inside noise) |

- **Steady-state numbers:** I excluded the irregular events at the start of the clip, where the spacing was 14 frames. Counting all 32 events gives 0.854.
- **Whole display:** it dips to about 0.886 at each steady update, 2–4 frames below 0.97 each time.
- **Camera:** it drifted at most 1 px.
- **Push rate:** 28 frames is 4.3 Hz, as predicted for the copy build.
- **Compared with the default:** 0.847 is the same as the default build's 0.862, within the spread.
- **Rod's eyes:** Rod saw the dip without measuring, so the copy path doesn't hide it.

**What the dip depends on:** the scene has to be evolving. The two builds that freeze it (`*speed: 0.01`) show no dip, even when I flip every pixel by 1 px. The two that let it scroll do. These don't matter:
- the write, bus load, supply or CPU load (the frozen builds do the same);
- which buffer the push reads, and when the copy runs;
- how many pixels change (the alternating build changes more);
- how much is lit;
- the picture's average level (the host check showed 0.18% change);
- CABC, with the earlier caveat.

I still don't have a mechanism. What's left is a property of smoothly evolving content, such as sub-pixel movement or small changes in grey level along the lines. I can't point to which.

**Next, a dose-response test.** We have the dip at speed 1.0 (0.85) and none at 0.01. A build at `*speed: 0.2` tells us the shape between them:
- If the dip shrinks smoothly with speed, it's proportional to how far the scene moves per push. A slower scroll is then a practical lever for #68, and the cost is that the plot scrolls slowly.
- If it stays near 0.85 until a threshold, the cause is something that switches on, and a slower scroll won't help.

It's one registry flag (`-DUP_SPEED=0.2`, behind the same pattern as the others), a build and a flash. Shall I build and flash it? The board is still on the shift-0 copy build.

S=/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-rod-build-stopwatch-screensaver/4c516cba-60f9-4ecc-8569-06298f6abd52/scratchpad; ffmpeg -v error -i $S/IMG_5869.MOV -vf scale=960:540,format=gray -f rawvideo $S/c960.raw -y; cat > $S/analyse7.py <<'EOF'
# /// script
# dependencies = ["numpy"]
# ///
import sys, numpy as np
S = sys.argv[1]
a = np.fromfile(S + "/c960.raw", np.uint8).reshape(-1, 540, 960)
print("frames", len(a))
def shift(ref, cur):
    w = np.outer(np.hanning(ref.shape[0]), np.hanning(ref.shape[1]))
    F = np.fft.fft2(ref * w) * np.conj(np.fft.fft2(cur * w))
    r = np.fft.ifft2(F / (np.abs(F) + 1e-6)).real
    y, x = np.unravel_index(r.argmax(), r.shape); h, wd = r.shape
    return (y if y < h // 2 else y - h, x if x < wd // 2 else x - wd)
for n, (y0, y1, x0, x1) in {"B": (500, 540, 300, 700), "T": (0, 30, 400, 640), "R": (180, 440, 925, 960)}.items():
    ref = a[0, y0:y1, x0:x1].astype(np.float32)
    sh = np.array([shift(ref, a[i, y0:y1, x0:x1].astype(np.float32)) for i in range(0, len(a), 20)])
    print(n, "dy", sh[:, 0].min(), sh[:, 0].max(), "dx", sh[:, 1].min(), sh[:, 1].max())
cx, cy, h, nb = 667, 299, 170, 12
roi = a[:, cy - h:cy + h, cx - h:cx + h].astype(np.float32)
whole = roi.mean(axis=(1, 2)); whole /= np.median(whole)
rowb = roi.reshape(len(a), nb, 2 * h // nb, 2 * h).mean(axis=(2, 3))
colb = roi.reshape(len(a), 2 * h, nb, 2 * h // nb).mean(axis=(1, 3))
print("whole-display: min %.3f, frames below 0.97: %d, below 0.985: %d" % (whole.min(), (whole < 0.97).sum(), (whole < 0.985).sum()))
# fold at the push period: scan 22-27 frames for the period whose folded profile has the largest dip
best = None
t = np.arange(len(whole))
for P in np.arange(22.0, 30.0, 0.02):
    ph = (t % P) / P; k = np.minimum((ph * int(P)).astype(int), int(P) - 1)
    prof = np.array([whole[k == j].mean() for j in range(int(P))])
    if best is None or np.median(prof) - prof.min() > best[0]: best = (np.median(prof) - prof.min(), P, prof)
d, P, prof = best
print("best fold period %.2f frames (%.2f Hz at 120 fps); folded whole-display profile:" % (P, 120 / P))
print(" ".join("%.3f" % v for v in prof))
print("folded dip depth: %.3f (min %.3f vs median %.3f)" % (d, prof.min(), np.median(prof)))
# per-band folded dip, both orientations
def folded_min(series, P):
    ph = (t % P) / P; k = np.minimum((ph * int(P)).astype(int), int(P) - 1)
    out = []
    for b in range(series.shape[1]):
        s = series[:, b] / np.median(series[:, b])
        pr = np.array([s[k == j].mean() for j in range(int(P))]); out.append(pr.min() / np.median(pr))
    return min(out)
print("dimmest folded band: rows %.3f  cols %.3f" % (folded_min(rowb, P), folded_min(colb, P)))
EOF
uv run --quiet $S/analyse7.py $S

Slowing the scroll nearly removes the dip. At speed 0.2 the dimmest band averages **0.986**, against 0.85 at the default speed, and you couldn't see it.

| Build | Scroll speed | Dimmest band vs settled | Visible to Rod |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Near-static (IMG_5865) | 0.01 | no dip (0.990) | no |
| **Slow (IMG_5869)** | **0.2** | **0.986 (about 1.4% dip)** | **no** |
| Sparse (IMG_5866) | 1.0, half the lines | 0.943 (5.7%) | no |
| Default (IMG_5864, IMG_5868) | 1.0 | 0.85–0.86 (14–15%) | yes |

- **Detail on this clip:** 36 pushes, dimmest row band 0.987, column band 0.985. The display is rotated here, so I measured bands in both orientations. The null windows, taken half a period later, sit at 0.995–0.997.
- **Is the 1.4% real?** Yes, but only just. It's about three times the null's 0.4%, and the fold at the right period finds it at 4.93 Hz while wrong periods find nothing. I wouldn't call it zero.
- **Camera drift:** 1 px or less.
- **Shape of the response:** 0.01 gives none, 0.2 gives about 1.4%, and 1.0 gives about 14%. A proportional dip would have been about 3% at 0.2, so it's less than proportional. With three points I can't say whether it's a threshold or a curve.
- **Mechanism:** the dip scales with how far the scene moves each push, though not with how many pixels change (the 1 px shift test). I still have no physical explanation.

**Decision for you:** the cost of the fix is that the plot scrolls five times slower, with a new row about every 6 s instead of 1.2 s. Speed 0.2 removes the visible fade, but the scroll may be too slow for what you want. A middle speed might keep a livelier scroll while the dip stays below what you can see. Your sparse build's 5.7% was invisible, and the default's 14% wasn't.

My recommendation is to try **0.5** next. It's one more build, flash and clip. If the fade is invisible at 0.5, that's the speed to ship. If it isn't, 0.2 stays as the choice.

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists

- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)

- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?

- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

````markdown

code()

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown

`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>

Wrong: user@example.com
```

```markdown
First paragraph.
```

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown

| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

Posted by Claude Code on Rod's behalf, at his request. This summarises one
working session; Rod filmed every clip and judged each build by eye.

## Summary

The dip follows a scene that is evolving. It is not the write to the panel, the
CPU or bus load, the number of pixels that change, how much is lit, or the
picture's average level. Slowing the scroll shrinks it in a straight line: at
`*speed: 0.3` it is 2.8% and Rod cannot see it. **The mechanism is still
unexplained.**

## Method

120 fps film, the method in `.claude/rules/device-display.md`. For each push,
the dimmest of 12 bands inside the display, against the same band's settled
brightness before the next push. Camera drift was 1 px or less in every clip.
Windows with no push give the noise floor (about 0.99 to 1.00 on the dense
build, looser on the sparse one).

## Results

| Build | Dimmest band | Dip | Rod, by eye |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Default, CABC off (`0x55 = 0`) | 0.862 (23 pushes) | 14% | visible |
| Default plus a copy of the canvas before each push | 0.847 (20) | 15% | visible |
| Near-static, `*speed: 0.01` | none (min 0.990) | 0 | invisible |
| Static scene, shifted 1 px on every other push | 0.977 (noise) | about 0 | invisible |
| Sparse, 20 rows of 50 points | 0.943 (40) | 5.7% | invisible |
| `*speed: 0.2` | 0.986 (36) | 1.4% | invisible, but "really slow" |
| `*speed: 0.3` | 0.972 (34) | 2.8% | invisible |
| `*speed: 0.5` | 0.938 (33) | 6.2% | visible |
| `*speed: 1.0` (default) | 0.85 to 0.86 | 14 to 15% | visible |

The speed points fit dip = 16.5% x (speed - 0.11). It predicted 3.1% for 0.3
before the clip was measured; 2.8% came back.

## What this rules out

- **The write itself.** The near-static build pushed the same 466 rows in
  32.3 ms at 5 Hz (serial log: `rows=466 push=32.3ms`) and did not dip. So bus
  load, supply sag from the QSPI and PSRAM traffic, and CPU load are out.
- **How many pixels change.** The shifted static scene changes every lit pixel
  every push (the 1 px alternation is visible in the film) and did not dip.
- **How much is lit.** The static build lights as many pixels as the default.
- **The average picture level.** On the host, the pushed frames' total
  brightness changes by 0.18% on average (0.82% at worst) from one frame to the
  next on the dense build, and by more on the sparse build (0.54%, 3.75%),
  which dips less.
- **Which buffer the push reads, or when it is copied.** The copy build still
  dips.
- **CABC**, with a caveat: I could not confirm the panel accepted the `0x55`
  write.

## Not known

- The mechanism. What is left is something about smoothly evolving content
  (sub-pixel movement of the lines, small grey-level changes along them).
- Why 5.7% on the sparse build was invisible to Rod while 6.2% on the dense
  build at 0.5 was not. Pulse rate (7.5 Hz against 4.9 Hz) and density probably
  matter as well as depth.
- One idea, untested: the hack moves by elapsed time, so motion per push is
  speed times the time between pushes. A faster step might cut the dip at the
  same apparent scroll speed. The sparse build fits roughly (14.5% x 0.67 x 0.5
  is about 4.8%, against 5.7% measured), but that is one point.

## Status

- Proposed fix: an override of `*speed: 0.3` for Unknown Pleasures. Not made
  yet. It would need the pinned frame hashes re-taken and the notes in
  `device-display.md` and `gl.md` updated.
- The probe builds (`-DCABC_OFF`, `-DALT_PROBE`, `-DUP_STATIC`, `-DUP_SPARSE`,
  `-DUP_SPEED`) are on the local branch `fix/68-cabc-off-probe`, not pushed.
- The board is running the pinned `*speed: 0.3` build.

You are giving an independent second opinion on a hardware debugging problem. Rod (the user) wants to know what experiments or explanations we have missed. Please think critically, and challenge my inferences rather than confirming them.

## The project and problem

Repo: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver (read AGENTS.md and .claude/rules/device-display.md, section "Reading a film of the display" and the Tearing / "Every push also dims the screen" bullets, plus .claude/rules/gl.md). It runs xscreensaver hacks on an M5Stack StopWatch (ESP32-S3, 466x466 round AMOLED, CO5300 panel driven over QSPI through M5GFX, which keeps a PSRAM framebuffer). Issue #68: on the Unknown Pleasures hack (thin white lines, TinyGL, 40 rows x 100 points, ~5 pushes/s, pushes are TE-synced full 466-row frames costing ~32 ms) every push dims the whole picture for about 25 ms (three frames at 120 fps), then it recovers. Rod sees it by eye as pulsing. Read the issue with: gh api repos/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/68 --jq '.body' and the comments (issues/68/comments). Our latest comment (id 6254752184) summarises this session.

## Evidence so far (filmed at 120 fps by phone; I measured each with the same pipeline)

Metric: per push, the dimmest of 12 bands inside the display divided by that band's settled brightness before the next push. No-push windows give the noise floor (about 0.99-1.00 on dense builds).

| Build | Dimmest band | Rod by eye |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default (speed 1.0), CABC off via 0x55=0 | 0.862 | visible |
| Default + copy of canvas before each push (shift 0) | 0.847 | visible |
| Near-static, `*speed: 0.01` (still pushes 466 rows at 5 Hz, serial-log confirmed) | none (0.990) | invisible |
| Static scene, whole picture shifted 1 px on every other push (changes every lit pixel each push; shift visible in film) | 0.977 (noise) | invisible |
| Sparse, 20 rows x 50 points, ~7.5 Hz | 0.943 | invisible |
| speed 0.2 | 0.986 | invisible, "really slow" |
| speed 0.3 | 0.972 | invisible |
| speed 0.5 | 0.938 | visible |
| speed 1.0 | ~0.85 | visible |

Dip is linear in speed: about 16.5% x (speed - 0.11). Host check: total brightness of successive pushed frames changes only 0.18% mean (0.82% max) on the dense build and 0.54%/3.75% on the sparse one, so average-picture-level (APL) limiting seems not to explain it.

My current inferences (challenge them): not the write itself, not bus/supply/CPU load (the static build does all of that), not number of changed pixels, not lit area, not APL, not the push path or buffer, not CABC (but I could not confirm the panel accepted the 0x55 write). The mechanism is unknown; what is left is "smoothly evolving content" (sub-pixel line movement, grey-level changes along anti-aliased lines). An untested idea: the hack moves by elapsed time, so motion per push = speed x time between pushes.

Open puzzle: sparse build dip 5.7% was invisible to Rod, dense 6.2% (speed 0.5) visible.

## Where things live

- Scratchpad (clips, scripts, logs): /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-rod-build-stopwatch-screensaver/4c516cba-60f9-4ecc-8569-06298f6abd52/scratchpad
  - Clips: IMG_5864 (CABC off, default), 5865 (near-static), 5866 (sparse), 5867 (static + 1 px alternation), 5868 (default + copy, shift 0), 5869 (speed 0.2), 5870 (speed 0.5), 5871 (speed 0.3). 120 fps content stored with 30 fps timestamps (frames are 1/120 s of real time).

  - serial_static.log, serial_alt.log: run logs.
- Code: the hack is firmware/src/hacks/unknownpleasures/unknownpleasures.c (byte-identical xscreensaver copy; how it uses `speed`, `tick`, and its line drawing is worth reading). Registry overrides are in firmware/src/hacks/registry.c. Push path is firmware/src/main.cpp (`present`, `sinkAll`) and firmware/src/core/push_plan.c. M5GFX's CO5300 driver is under firmware/.pio/libdeps/stopwatch/M5GFX/src/lgfx/v1/panel/ (Panel_CO5300.hpp, Panel_AMOLED.*) and the StopWatch panel subclass is in M5GFX.cpp near line 726. The GL layer is firmware/src/glshim.
- Branch fix/68-cabc-off-probe holds the probe flags (-DCABC_OFF, -DALT_PROBE, -DALT_SHIFT_PX, -DUP_STATIC, -DUP_SPARSE, -DUP_SPEED). It is local and unpushed.

## What I want from you

1. Your best explanations for why the dip depends on scene evolution (and scales linearly with speed) yet not on pixels changed, lit area or APL. Consider panel-side behaviour (CO5300 and AMOLED drivers: brightness/gamma compensation, dynamic ELVSS or IR-drop compensation, AOD/idle features, register defaults M5GFX leaves alone, e.g. 0x53, 0x55, 0x63), GRAM and scan interaction (tearing, TE timing), the sub-pixel anti-aliasing of the lines, and the possibility that part of this is a camera or encoder effect. Rank them.
2. For each, the cheapest discriminating experiment (build flag, host-only test, or film), with what each outcome would mean. Prefer experiments that need no flash. Say which ones need Rod to flash or film.
3. Any flaw in my measurement method or in my reading of the table above (for example confounds between builds: push rate, density, timing against TE, band orientation).
4. A recommendation: is shipping `*speed: 0.3` (dip 2.8%, invisible to Rod, plot scrolls at 30% of upstream speed) a sensible stopping point, and is there a cheaper lever that keeps a livelier scroll?

  ### Headline: two inferences in the table do not hold, and the data fit one mechanism
  
  **1. The ALT probe did not "change every lit pixel".** `altCopy()` in `firmware/src/main.cpp` shifts the canvas *right* (horizontally). Unknown Pleasures' lines are near-horizontal, so a 1 px horizontal shift relights few pixels. Measured on a host dump of the real hack (index 52, `scratchpad/shift_probe.py`): lit pixels 24,748; horizontal 1 px shift: 23.6% newly lit; vertical 1 px shift: 50.5% (lines are ~2 px thick, median vertical run 2); a frame ~0.2 s later: 79.8%; ~1 s later: 94.9%. Row spacing 14 px, so at speed 1.0 lines move ~2.3 px per 200 ms push, i.e. nearly every lit pixel is freshly lit each push. So "not the number of changed pixels" was never tested.
  
  **2. There is no anti-aliasing.** TinyGL defines `GL_LINE_SMOOTH` but implements nothing (`grep` in `tinygl/src`, `glshim.c`: `glLineWidth` is a no-op). Lines are hard 2 px strokes that step by whole pixels. "Smoothly evolving content" is really "fraction of lines that stepped since the last push".
  
  **3. The dip is uniform across every line, not a seam, and it is whole-screen.** I re-ran the clips with a row-by-row comparison (`scratchpad/seam_or_uniform.py`, same event detection as analyse11):
  
  | Clip | row band | col band | whole frame | lit rows dimmed >5% |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 5864 default | 0.869 | 0.854 | 0.911 | 99% |
  | 5870 speed 0.5 | 0.938 | 0.934 | 0.952 | 86% |
  | 5867 ALT (horizontal) | 0.981 | 0.974 | 0.988 | 0% (but a ~1.2% uniform deficit at frame 0, sweeping down) |
  
  Deficit per band peaks at frame 0 in the top half and frame +1 in the bottom half (travels with the write), then decays 3%, 2%, 1% over frames +2..+4. The ALT clip's push period was 28.3 camera frames (4.2 Hz), not 5 Hz: the copy slowed the push.
  
  ### Ranked explanations
  
  1. **Pixel turn-on transient (LTPS TFT hysteresis / storage-cap charging from black), most likely.** A pixel going black to white under-emits for a refresh or two; white to black is instant. Dip ∝ fraction of lit pixels that were black in the previous frame: ~90% at speed 1.0 (whole 9%), ~55% at 0.5 (4.8%), 24% for ALT (1.2%), ~0 static. Travels with the write, decays over ~30 ms, independent of APL, TE phase, bus load. Fits every row. Inference, not proof.
  2. **Driver-side dynamic compensation (ELVSS/IR-drop, ACL)**: would respond to APL or load, which barely change; would not sweep with the write. Unlikely.
  3. **Tearing seam / camera effect**: ruled out by the uniform per-line deficit and by Rod seeing it.
  4. **CABC**: moot; M5GFX never writes 0x55 and DCS default is off; CABC tracks APL anyway.

  - **Vertical ALT shift on the static build** (one edit to `altCopy`: shift rows by 2 instead of columns): every lit pixel becomes new. Prediction under #1: full ~14% band dip at speed 0.01. If it stays flat, #1 is dead.
  - **`-DUP_SPEED=2.0`**: #1 predicts saturation near 14-15% (nothing left to relight); the linear fit predicts ~31%.
  - Host-only, already done: the shift counts above.
  
  ### Method notes
  
  Plot the dip against px moved per push (speed × push period) or newly-lit fraction, not `speed`; the ALT and sparse builds pushed at different rates. Report the whole-frame dip (9%) alongside the dimmest band: the band minimum over 12 bands adds a small downward bias, though the half-period null covers it. The 0.11 intercept is probably the noise floor plus integer stepping, not a real threshold.
  
  ### Recommendation
  
  `*speed: 0.3` works because only ~35% of lines step per push; it is a sound stopping point if Rod accepts the pace. A livelier lever that follows from #1: in the push path, keep a copy of the last pushed frame (the ALT buffer already exists) and push steady lit pixels at ~87% while pixels that were black last frame go at 100%, i.e. a one-frame pre-emphasis; or OR the previous frame in (a 1-frame trail, thicker-looking lines). Either is per-hack, needs no hack or shim edits, and costs the copy (~28 ms at present, absorbable by the overlap path). Prove the vertical-shift experiment first, then ask Rod which look he wants.
  
  Checks run: `pio run -e dump` (host), dumps `scratchpad/up_{a,b,c,d}.raw`, `shift_probe.py`, ffmpeg decodes `g5864.raw`, `g5867.raw`, `l5870.raw`, `seam_or_uniform.py` on each. Not checked: the CO5300 datasheet (not available), the device.

"""How many lit pixels change under a 1 px horizontal shift, a 1 px vertical
shift, and between two dumped Unknown Pleasures frames."""
import sys
import numpy as np

W = H = 466


def load(p):
    a = np.fromfile(p, dtype=np.uint16)
    a = a[: W * H].reshape(H, W)
    sw = ((a & 0xFF) << 8) | (a >> 8)  # canvas is byte-swapped
    r = (sw >> 11) & 31
    g = (sw >> 5) & 63
    b = sw & 31
    return (r * 255 // 31 + g * 255 // 63 + b * 255 // 31) / 3.0


def lit(img):
    return img > 40


def report(name, a, b):
    la, lb = lit(a), lit(b)
    changed = np.count_nonzero(la != lb)
    newly = np.count_nonzero(lb & ~la)
    print(f"{name}: lit_a={la.sum()} lit_b={lb.sum()} changed={changed} "

content.text:
The subagent found a real error in my work. I checked its claims myself, and its numbers hold up.

**My alternating-frames probe didn't test what I said it did.** I told you it "changes every lit pixel". But `altCopy()` shifts the picture one pixel sideways, and Unknown Pleasures' lines are nearly horizontal, so a sideways shift relights few pixels. I re-ran the subagent's script on its host dumps of the real hack:

| Comparison | Pixels newly lit, as a share of lit |
| --- | --- |
| 1 px horizontal shift (my probe) | 23.6% |
| 1 px vertical shift | 50.5% |
| A frame 0.2 s later (one push at speed 1.0) | 79.8% |
| A frame 1 s later | 94.9% |

- **Consequence:** "the dip isn't the number of changed pixels" was never tested. At the default speed nearly every lit pixel is freshly lit on each push, and my probe relit about a quarter.
- **No anti-aliasing:** `glLineWidth` in the glshim is a no-op, and the lines are hard strokes about 2 px thick that step by whole pixels. My "sub-pixel movement" idea was wrong. The grey levels in the dumps come from shading.
- **Whole screen:** the subagent's per-line check says the dip is the same on every line and sweeps down with the write, so it isn't a tearing seam.

**The subagent's leading explanation (inference, not proof):** a pixel going from black to lit under-emits for a frame or two, and a pixel going from lit to black is instant. That makes the dip proportional to how many lit pixels were black in the previous push.
- Default speed gives about 85–90% newly lit and a 9% whole-frame dip.
- Speed 0.5 gives about 55% and 4.8%.
- My shifted probe gives 24% and 1.2%.
- The static build gives about 0 and no dip.

That fits every clip, including the linear speed response, because motion per push divided by the line thickness is roughly the newly-lit fraction. The speed fit's intercept of 0.11 is probably noise plus whole-pixel stepping, not a real threshold.

**Experiments to discriminate**
1. **Vertical shift on the static build (my recommendation).** Shift the rows by 2 px instead of the columns, so every lit pixel becomes newly lit. The mechanism predicts a dip near the default's 14% at speed 0.01. A flat result kills the idea. It's a one-line edit to my probe, then a build, a flash and a clip from you.
2. **`-DUP_SPEED=2.0`.** The mechanism predicts saturation near 14–15%, because nothing is left to relight. The straight-line fit predicts about 31%.

**If the mechanism holds, a livelier lever exists:** in the push path, keep the last pushed frame and push steady lit pixels at about 87% while pixels that were black go at 100%, a one-frame pre-emphasis. Alternatively OR the previous frame in for a one-frame trail, which gives thicker-looking lines. Either is per-hack, needs no hack or shim edits, and would be your call on the look. Prove experiment 1 first.

**The subagent's view on shipping `*speed: 0.3`:** a sound stopping point if you accept the pace, because only about a third of lines step per push.

**Two things need your say-so:**
1. **Correct the issue.** The comment I posted says the shifted-scene probe changed every lit pixel, and so rules out pixel count. That's wrong. I'd post a short correction that quotes the numbers above. Shall I?
2. **Run experiment 1.** It's a build, a flash and a clip from you.

1	# Unknown Pleasures flicker: independent review
2	
3	Rod, the evidence favours a problem associated with changing the picture,
4	especially moving thin lines across pixels. It does not yet identify the
5	physical mechanism. I would keep investigating before adopting speed 0.3 as
6	the permanent solution: that slows the animation, and the existing evidence
7	does not establish that normal-speed motion must flicker.
8	
9	Reviewed on 18 October 2026 at commit `86290b6`: issue #68 and its comments,
10	Entire session `4c516cba-60f9-4ecc-8569-06298f6abd52`, scratchpad analysis
11	scripts and data, application and installed M5GFX source, and the CO5300
12	datasheet. Historical observations below come from Rod's recorded feedback
13	and the prior session; new measurements are identified separately.
14	
15	## What survives an independent check
16	
17	I reanalysed the existing `g5864.raw` baseline video data, using a central
18	300-by-300 crop and 12 horizontal bands. Across 22 selected update events:
19	
20	| Measurement | Mean ratio to settled image |
21	| --- | --- |
22	| Dimmest band | 0.863 |
23	| Dimmest band versus the darker of old/new settled bands | 0.866 |
24	| Whole central crop | 0.899 |
25	| External mat reference patch | 0.998 |
26	
27	This reproduces the reported dip. Simply comparing an old frame with a
28	brighter new frame does not account for it. Ordinary whole-camera exposure
29	changes are also less convincing when the external reference stays steady.
30	Rod's reports of visible flicker are independent evidence that the symptom
31	is not solely a camera artefact.
32	
33	These are ratios of decoded camera values, not calibrated light output.
34	The event detector selects minima, so this is a reproduction of the existing
35	measurement, not an independent measurement of push timing. Rolling shutter,
36	camera processing and the mixture of old/new spatial content remain relevant.
37	The 14% figure describes the worst band, not uniform dimming of every pixel.
38	
39	## Conclusions I would push back on
40	
41	### The one-pixel shift does not rule out pixel-transition effects
42	
43	The probe shifts right, along the predominantly horizontal strokes in the
44	native image. Moving every source pixel does not mean every destination
45	pixel changes value: neighbouring points along a line often have similar
46	values. Vertical motion crosses those strokes and is a different control.
47	
48	New measurements on the saved `up_a.raw`, with lit defined as decoded mean
49	RGB greater than 40 out of 255:
50	
51	| Shift | Newly lit fraction of target lit pixels | Absolute intensity change / original total |
52	| --- | --- | --- |
53	| One pixel horizontally | 19.78% | 0.592 |
54	| One pixel vertically | 54.41% | 1.402 |
55	
56	These are illustrative measurements on one saved host image, not a capture
57	of the exact frame in the device experiment. They nevertheless disprove the
58	general reasoning that shifting the image changes every lit pixel's value.
59	The issue's statement that the amount of pixel change is ruled out should
60	be withdrawn.
61	
62	There is also a decoding trap: scratchpad `shift_probe.py` swaps the bytes
63	again, whereas `dump_main.c` already writes ordinary little-endian RGB565.
64	The measurements here decode that documented dump format without a swap.
65	
66	### Static traffic weakens one power hypothesis; it does not exclude power
67	
68	The near-static experiment is strong evidence against an unconditional
69	blanking event on every full-frame write, or a dip caused only by the amount
70	of bus traffic. It does not exclude transition-dependent panel current,
71	transient supply behaviour, or effects that depend on the data pattern.
72	
73	Similarly, near-constant total brightness in completed host frames does not
74	bound instantaneous current during a display update. Neither the time
75	constant nor the transfer function of a hypothetical limiter was measured.
76	Rejecting every APL/current-limit explanation because endpoint brightness
77	changes by less than 1% is too strong. Those explanations are unproven, not
78	eliminated.
79	
80	### The CO5300 register semantics matter
81	
82	The detailed CO5300 command description calls `0x55` **Auto Current Limit
83	(ACL)**: `00` disables it and `11` enables it. Some generic-interface text in
84	the same document calls it CABC, so the naming confusion is understandable.
85	The existing `0x55 = 0` probe targets ACL, but acceptance was not verified.
86	See the [CO5300 datasheet, printed page 190][datasheet].
87	
88	The installed M5GFX `Panel_CO5300.hpp` initialises `0x53` to `0x20`, which
89	already leaves the documented DD dimming bit clear. The datasheet describes
90	DD in connection with brightness-control changes; its existence is not
91	evidence that normal RAM writes cause this dip. The
92	[upstream initialisation][driver] matches the installed values.
93	
94	Crucially, installed `Panel_AMOLED.hpp` implements `readCommand()` and
95	`readData()` as stubs returning zero. A zero read through those methods
96	would prove nothing. Use a supported physical read path or a logic-analyser
97	trace; a deliberate visible brightness change through the same command path
98	can validate transport, but cannot alone prove ACL support.
99	
100	### Animation speed and push frequency are separate variables
101	
102	The recent `UP_SPEED` experiments reduce the hack's scrolling speed, not
103	directly its refresh frequency. The source computes motion from elapsed
104	time. At similar frame rates, speed 0.3 means smaller changes between images.
105	That is different from slowing pushes while preserving animation speed.
106	
107	The sparse build changes geometry, render time, frame rate and image density
108	together. It is encouraging, but cannot establish which variable helped.
109	The fitted speed/dip line is useful interpolation over the tested points,
110	not a physical law or a reliable extrapolation to other frame rates.
111	
112	## Most useful next experiments
113	
114	### 1. Replay two fixed frames with a stationary brightness reference
115	
116	Capture two consecutive device-rendered frames from the flickering build,
117	then replay them without rendering. Preserve the current write path, TE
118	offset and brightness. Include identical small grey and white reference
119	patches at several screen heights, outside the moving scene but inside the
120	written area. Start at the existing cadence.
121	
122	Compare `A A A A` with `A B A B`. Then hold each image for several pushes:
123	`A A A A B B B B`. Log the actual flush start/end and frame identity. This
124	separates content changes, repeated writes and rendering activity.
125	
126	- Only A/B transitions dip: investigate the changed pixel values and their
127	  scan timing; repeated transport is insufficient to trigger it.
128	- Unchanged reference patches dip too: a global or row-wide emission/current
129	  effect becomes much more plausible.
130	- References stay steady while moving strokes lose light: investigate
